title: Radiofrequency endometrial ablation for menorrhagia using a mesh electrode
article_subtype: Health technology assessment and benefit assessment
condition_or_topic: Radiofrequency endometrial ablation using a mesh electrode for menorrhagia
clinical_background: Heavy menstrual bleeding is a common menstrual disorder, although terminology and definitions vary. One definition distinguishes menorrhagia, involving prolonged (> 7 to 10 days) and increased menstruation, from hypermenorrhoea, involving increased menstruation of normal duration; increased blood loss is defined as > 80 ml. Other definitions emphasize the effect of bleeding on quality of life. This report uses menorrhagia to encompass any heavy menstrual bleeding. Fibroids and polyps are possible causes, but the cause is often unknown. Prostaglandins may contribute to its pathogenesis, and adenomyosis uteri is often associated with menorrhagia and dysmenorrhoea. Clinical practice guidelines identify drug treatment, particularly hormonal therapy or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, as the first therapeutic option. Surgery may be considered when drug treatment does not adequately reduce bleeding, is contraindicated, or is declined; surgical procedures are suitable only when there is no further desire to have children. Uterus-preserving options include endometrial resection and ablation. Hysterectomy provides a definitive reduction in bleeding but is more invasive and may be considered after an unsatisfactory response to endometrial ablation. Adenomyosis uteri is considered a risk factor for inadequate success of endometrial ablation.
objectives: Assess the benefit of radiofrequency endometrial ablation using a mesh electrode against loop resection and/or rollerball ablation and balloon ablation, focusing on patient-relevant outcomes in patients with menorrhagia and a medical indication for ablative therapy.
clinical_question: In patients with menorrhagia and a medical indication for ablative therapy (P), does radiofrequency endometrial ablation using a mesh electrode (I), compared with loop resection and/or rollerball ablation or balloon ablation (C), provide greater benefit or cause greater harm on patient-relevant outcomes, including morbidity, health-related quality of life, adverse events, and mortality (O)?
interpretation: Across patient-relevant outcomes, the assessment finds a hint of greater benefit for RF ablation than for L / R. Bleeding severity, the principal symptom, appears to improve comparably with the two procedures; the advantage for RF ablation rests on a hint of less dysmenorrhoea and a hint of less harm regarding AEs, chiefly intraoperative complications. Against balloon ablation, the assessment finds an indication of greater benefit for RF ablation, supported by proof of greater benefit for bleeding severity and a hint of greater benefit for PMS. The remaining assessed outcomes provide no hint of greater benefit or harm in either comparison where data were available; this does not establish that the procedures are equivalent for those outcomes.
clinical_implications: For patients with menorrhagia who have an indication for ablative therapy, the assessment identifies differences between RF ablation and the two comparators in patient-relevant outcomes, while retaining different levels of certainty for each comparison.

The uncertainty about surgical re-interventions has limited influence on the overall assessment because hysterectomies and re-ablations were comparatively infrequent in both groups up to 3 years after RF ablation versus L / R and up to 10 years after RF ablation versus balloon ablation.
A comparative judgment about harm from RF ablation versus balloon ablation remains difficult because the completeness of AE ascertainment or reporting is uncertain.
limitations: Both RF ablation versus L / R studies had a high risk of bias across outcomes, including unclear concealment of allocation and lack of blinding of patients and treating staff.

Among the RF ablation versus balloon ablation studies, Abbott 2003, COAT, and Penninx 2016 had a high risk of bias across outcomes. Some outcomes and follow-up points in Bongers 2004 also had a high risk of bias.

For RF ablation versus L / R, the studies planned to assess health-related quality of life but did not report results, and they did not collect mortality data. Some reported outcomes could not be used because reporting was inadequate.

For RF ablation versus L / R, AEs could not be combined across Cooper 2002's 4 reporting periods to obtain an overall proportion of affected patients. In Corson 2000, systematic ascertainment and complete reporting of AEs were unclear.

For RF ablation versus balloon ablation, outcome definitions, instruments, or measurement times sometimes prevented pooling; missing data or inadequate outcome assessment also made some reported results unusable.

In Abbott 2003 and Penninx 2016, it is unclear whether AEs were fully ascertained or reported. In Bongers 2004 and COAT, incomplete ascertainment or reporting outside the immediate postoperative period is considered likely.

An additional, previously unpublished study could not be definitively judged relevant because its RF ablation procedure was unspecified; the assessment states that this uncertainty does not change its overall conclusion.
open_questions: The available evidence does not establish with sufficient certainty whether RF ablation and L / R have comparable effects on surgical re-interventions.
The available evidence does not establish with sufficient certainty whether RF ablation and balloon ablation have comparable effects on surgical re-interventions.
Because AE ascertainment or reporting may be incomplete, comparative harm from RF ablation and balloon ablation remains difficult to determine.
study_design: Systematic benefit assessment restricted to randomized controlled trials (RCTs), with meta-analyses when methodological conditions permitted. The assessment compared radiofrequency endometrial ablation using a mesh electrode with other endometrial ablation or resection procedures used in German health care. No restriction was imposed on study duration.

population.description: Patients with menorrhagia and a medical indication for ablative therapy. The included trials enrolled premenopausal women without a wish for further childbearing. Cooper 2002 enrolled women aged 25 to 50 years, Corson 2000 enrolled women aged 30 to 49 years, and COAT enrolled women aged 25 years and older; the other balloon-ablation trials did not specify an age range.
inclusion_criteria: Cooper 2002 and Corson 2000 required a PBAC score of at least 150 points and either unsuccessful prior drug therapy, a contraindication to drug therapy, or refusal of drug therapy.
Bongers 2004 and Penninx 2016 required a PBAC score ≥ 150 points; Abbott 2003 required a PBAC score > 150 points.
COAT enrolled women whose menstrual bleeding affected their quality of life and required unsuccessful prior drug therapy.
population.care_setting: Settings varied by study. Corson 2000 used an outpatient practice or hospital for RF ablation and a hospital for L / R. COAT and Penninx 2016 treated patients in outpatient practices; Abbott 2003 and Bongers 2004 used hospital-based outpatient settings. Cooper 2002 did not specify a setting.

interventions: RF ablation of the endometrium using a mesh electrode; Cooper 2002 used NovaSure, Corson 2000 used Vesta, and all 4 trials against balloon ablation used NovaSure.
comparators: Loop resection combined with rollerball ablation in Cooper 2002 and Corson 2000.
Balloon ablation in Abbott 2003, Bongers 2004, COAT, and Penninx 2016; the control groups in Abbott 2003 and Bongers 2004 underwent curettage immediately before ablation.
statistical_methods: The report did not assign outcomes to primary and secondary categories. It assessed patient-relevant morbidity, including bleeding severity and dysmenorrhoea; health-related quality of life; adverse events, particularly intraoperative and postoperative complications; and mortality. For each outcome, results were preferentially presented at 12 months and at the latest measurement time point. Adverse events and pain were also presented during or shortly after treatment when available. Individual-study results were compared; meta-analyses, sensitivity analyses, and examinations of effect modifiers were undertaken when methodological requirements were met. Conclusions were graded as proof, indication, hint, or no hint of greater benefit or harm.
follow_up: No study-duration restriction applied. Cooper 2002 and Corson 2000 followed patients for up to 36 months after surgery. Follow-up was 1 year in Abbott 2003 and Penninx 2016, 5 years in COAT, and 10 years in Bongers 2004.

main_conclusion: Across outcomes, the authors find a hint of greater benefit for radiofrequency endometrial ablation using a mesh electrode compared with combined loop resection and rollerball ablation, and an indication of greater benefit compared with balloon ablation. The respective findings are driven by dysmenorrhoea and less harm regarding adverse events, chiefly intraoperative complications, in the first comparison, and by bleeding severity and premenstrual syndrome in the second.
narrative_summary:
This benefit assessment examined radiofrequency endometrial ablation using a mesh electrode for patients with menorrhagia who had a medical indication for ablative treatment. It included 6 randomized controlled trials: 2 compared radiofrequency ablation with combined loop resection and rollerball ablation, and 4 compared it with balloon ablation. Outcomes focused on symptoms, daily functioning, health-related quality of life, adverse events and mortality.

Against loop resection and rollerball ablation, the evidence provides a hint of improvement in dysmenorrhoea and a hint of less harm from adverse events, chiefly through fewer intraoperative complications. Bleeding severity, the leading symptom, appeared to benefit comparably from either procedure; the assessment found no hint of greater benefit or harm for this outcome or for premenstrual syndrome, daily activities and surgical re-interventions. Health-related quality-of-life and mortality results were unavailable.

Against balloon ablation, the evidence provides proof of greater benefit for bleeding severity and a hint of greater benefit for premenstrual syndrome. It provides no hint of greater benefit or harm for the other assessed outcomes, including surgical re-interventions and adverse events; daily-activity data were unusable. The authors note uncertainty about comparative adverse-event reporting in these studies. Overall, their conclusions favour radiofrequency ablation with a hint of greater benefit over loop resection and rollerball ablation, and an indication of greater benefit over balloon ablation.

safety_results.overall_adverse_events: An overall patient-level AE rate could not be calculated for RF ablation versus L / R because Cooper 2002 reported separate periods without identifying patients with events in multiple periods. For RF ablation versus balloon ablation, incomplete or uncertain AE recording prevented a reliable comparative assessment; the report found no hint of greater or less harm.
notable_adverse_events: In Cooper 2002, the RF-ablation group had 1 intraoperative bradycardia of questionable patient relevance.
In Corson 2000, the RF-ablation group had 1 electrode-balloon slippage into a caesarean scar and 1 muscle fasciculation intraoperatively; both were judged not patient-relevant.

Across the L / R control groups in Cooper 2002 and Corson 2000, intraoperative events in 10 patients comprised 4 uterine perforations, 4 cervical tears, 1 cervical stenosis and 1 fluid overload. The patient with fluid overload reportedly had no resulting complications, but its direct patient relevance remained unclear because symptom information was unavailable.
In Cooper 2002, AEs at < 24 hours after surgery, excluding the intraoperative period, affected 6 (3.4%) RF-ablation patients and 4 patients (4.4%) in the L / R group.
In Cooper 2002, AEs at > 24 hours to 2 weeks after surgery affected 4 (2.3%) RF-ablation patients and 6 (6.7%) L / R patients.
In Cooper 2002, AEs at > 2 weeks to 1 year after surgery affected 19 (10.9%) RF-ablation patients and 15 patients (16.7%) in the L / R group.
Corson 2000 reported 4 postoperative events each in the two control groups, without specifying the period or the number of affected patients; none was recognizably serious or life-threatening.

Abbott 2003 reported no serious intraoperative complications. By 1 year, suspected endometritis treated with oral antibiotics occurred in 2 / 37 (5%) RF-ablation patients and 2 / 18 (11%) balloon-ablation patients.
Abbott 2003 reported severe pain caused by haematometra in one RF-ablation patient 4 months after treatment.
Abbott 2003 reported pregnancy followed by incomplete miscarriage in one balloon-ablation patient 8 months after treatment.

Bongers 2004 reported no complications during treatment. At 10 years, 1 / 69 (1%) evaluated RF-ablation patients had undergone hysterectomy because cervical stenosis caused haematometra and cycle-related pain; no AEs were reported among the 35 evaluated balloon-ablation patients. Other possible AEs appeared among hysterectomy reasons, but their figures were not included in the extract.

In COAT, postoperative complications affected 2 RF-ablation patients out of 42 and 2 balloon-ablation patients out of 39: 1 RF-ablation patient had severe pain radiating to the leg; 1 patient in each group stayed in hospital for 1 night for postoperative pain control; and 1 balloon-ablation patient had a vasovagal reaction.
COAT reported no serious intraoperative complications. Up to 3 months, endometritis occurred in 2 / 42 RF-ablation patients (5%) and 5 / 39 balloon-ablation patients (13%).
Penninx 2016 reported no complications, without specifying whether this covered a particular period or the entire 1 year of follow-up.

secondary_results: Information retrieval identified 6 eligible RCTs: Cooper 2002 and Corson 2000 compared RF ablation with L / R; Abbott 2003, Bongers 2004, COAT and Penninx 2016 compared it with balloon ablation. No planned or ongoing studies were identified.

For RF ablation versus L / R, none of the 8 Menstrual Impact Questionnaire items showed a statistically significant difference at 1 year in Cooper 2002. The report found no hint of greater benefit or harm for activities of daily living.

For RF ablation versus L / R, usable data on other types of pain were unavailable. Health-related quality-of-life assessment was planned in both studies, but neither reported results; mortality data were not collected.

For RF ablation versus balloon ablation, activities-of-daily-living data were unusable. In COAT, missing participant data or inadequate outcome assessment or description also rendered several reported outcomes or assessment times unusable.

For RF ablation versus balloon ablation, the studies used different definitions or measurements of bleeding reduction, dysmenorrhoea, menstrual duration and quality of life. The report therefore did not pool results where it considered them insufficiently comparable.
For RF ablation versus balloon ablation, no informative pooled analysis of re-ablation at 1 year was undertaken because only 1 event occurred in 1 study.

The report found no hint of greater benefit or harm with RF ablation versus balloon ablation for dysmenorrhoea/pain, depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, state of health, postoperative pain, workdays missed after surgery, surgical re-interventions, health-related quality of life or mortality.

The report could not establish with sufficient certainty whether surgical re-intervention benefit was comparable between RF ablation and either comparator, although hysterectomies and re-ablations were described as comparatively infrequent.

Abstracts described an unpublished study conducted in China comparing an unspecified RF ablation technique with L / R. Its relevance could not be resolved from available information, and it did not change the report's overall conclusion.

document_sections.heading: Key statement Research question
document_sections.content: The assessment examines radiofrequency endometrial ablation with a mesh electrode against loop resection and/or rollerball ablation and balloon ablation, which are used in German care. Its population has menorrhagia and a medical indication for ablative treatment. Patient-relevant outcomes are the focus.

document_sections.heading: Conclusion Comparison of radiofrequency ablation versus loop resection / rollerball ablation
document_sections.content: Two studies compared radiofrequency ablation with combined loop resection and rollerball ablation. The evidence gives a hint of greater benefit for dysmenorrhoea and a hint of less harm for adverse events (AEs) with radiofrequency ablation; the harm finding chiefly reflects fewer intraoperative complications. There is no hint of greater benefit or harm for bleeding severity, premenstrual syndrome, activities of daily living, or surgical re-interventions. The procedures appear to offer comparable benefit for bleeding severity. Other morbidity outcomes, health-related quality of life, and mortality had no available data and thus no hint of greater benefit or harm. Considering outcomes together, the evidence gives a hint of greater benefit with radiofrequency ablation.

document_sections.heading: Comparison of radiofrequency ablation versus balloon ablation
document_sections.content: Four studies assessed this comparison. The evidence provides proof of greater benefit for bleeding severity and a hint of greater benefit for premenstrual syndrome with radiofrequency ablation. It provides no hint of greater benefit or harm for dysmenorrhoea/pain, depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, state of health, postoperative pain, workdays missed after surgery, surgical re-interventions, AEs, health-related quality of life, or mortality. Activities of daily living had no usable data and likewise no hint of greater benefit or harm. Across outcomes, the evidence provides an indication of greater benefit with radiofrequency ablation.

document_sections.heading: 1 Background
document_sections.content: Heavy menstrual bleeding is among the most common menstrual disorders, although terminology varies across the literature. Under a cited definition, menorrhagia means menstruation that is both increased and prolonged (> 7 to 10 days), whereas hypermenorrhoea means increased menstruation of normal duration; increased loss means > 80 ml. A cited NICE definition instead centres on excessive menstrual loss that disrupts physical, social, emotional, or material quality of life. This report uses menorrhagia for any heavy menstrual bleeding. Fibroids and polyps are possible causes, but the cause is often unknown. Prostaglandins appear to contribute to pathogenesis. Adenomyosis uteri involves endometriosis of the myometrium and is often associated with menorrhagia and dysmenorrhoea. Cited clinical guidelines place drug treatment first, particularly hormonal therapy with oral contraceptives or hormonal intrauterine devices, or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Surgery may be considered if medication does not sufficiently relieve bleeding, is contraindicated, or is declined; surgical options suit patients who no longer wish to have children. Endometrial ablation and resection preserve the uterus. First-generation procedures use hysteroscopic control; most second-generation procedures do not. The former include monopolar or bipolar loop resection, often with rollerball ablation, and laser ablation. The latter include radiofrequency (RF), fluid-filled thermal balloon, microwave, and hydrothermal ablation. RF ablation, loop resection / rollerball ablation (L / R), and balloon ablation are commonly used in Germany. Hysterectomy definitively reduces bleeding but is more invasive than ablation and may be considered after an unsatisfactory ablation result. Adenomyosis uteri is considered a risk factor for inadequate success of endometrial ablation.

document_sections.heading: 2 Research question
document_sections.content: The investigation assesses the benefit of RF endometrial ablation with a mesh electrode against loop resection and/or rollerball ablation and balloon ablation, the relevant endometrial procedures commonly used in German care. It concerns patients with menorrhagia who have a medical indication for ablation and concentrates on patient-relevant outcomes.

document_sections.heading: 3 Methods
document_sections.content: Eligible patients had menorrhagia and a medical indication for ablative therapy. The intervention was RF endometrial ablation with a mesh electrode; comparators were loop resection and/or rollerball ablation and balloon ablation. Outcomes comprised morbidity, including bleeding severity and dysmenorrhoea; health-related quality of life; AEs, particularly intraoperative and postoperative complications; and mortality, including procedure-related death. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were eligible, with no study-duration restriction. A parallel search for systematic reviews covered MEDLINE, including the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, the health technology assessment database, and NICE and Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality websites. Investigators checked for at least 1 eligible, current, high-quality review that could underpin study identification. If one existed, they supplemented its coverage with a search for later studies; otherwise, they searched without a date restriction. Primary-study searches covered MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials. Other sources included registries, manufacturer inquiries, public regulatory documents, Federal Joint Committee submissions, reference lists, consultation documents, and author inquiries. Two individuals independently selected studies and resolved differences through discussion. Data went into standardized tables. Across-outcome and outcome-specific risk of bias were each rated low or high to assess qualitative certainty, and individual-study results were described by outcome. Results were preferably presented at 12 months and at the latest assessment; available AE and pain results during or soon after treatment were also included. Meta-analyses, sensitivity analyses, and examination of effect modifiers depended on methodological suitability. Outcome conclusions used the certainty grades proof, indication, hint, or none of those 3. When data were absent or could not support the other grades, the conclusion was no hint of greater benefit or harm. Benefit and harm were then considered across outcomes.

document_sections.heading: 4.1 Results of information retrieval
document_sections.content: One systematic review was judged current and high-quality and used to identify primary studies. The search found 6 relevant RCTs and no planned or ongoing studies. The final search occurred on 19 March 2021. The Appendix provides database and registry search strategies. Table 1 identifies the studies and the types of available study documents.

document_sections.heading: 4.2 Characteristics of the studies included in the assessment
document_sections.content: Of the 6 included RF ablation studies, Cooper 2002 and Corson 2000 compared it with L / R. Abbott 2003, Bongers 2004, COAT, and Penninx 2016 compared it with balloon ablation. Study characteristics are organized by comparator.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.1 Comparison of RF ablation versus L / R
document_sections.content: Cooper 2002 and Corson 2000 each compared RF ablation against loop resection combined with rollerball ablation. Both were multicentre North American studies. A publication cited for the Cooper 2002 sample-size calculation indicates a noninferiority question, unlike Corson 2000. Cooper 2002 randomized 265 patients and Corson 2000 randomized 276; both followed patients for up to 36 months after surgery. Initial allocation was 2:1 in both studies, but Corson 2000 changed to 1:1 during the study. Participants were premenopausal women with menorrhagia, no further wish for children, and ages between 25 and 50 years in Cooper 2002 or 30 and 49 years in Corson 2000. Eligibility required PBAC ≥ 150 points and either unsuccessful prior drug therapy, a contraindication, or refusal of drug therapy. Cooper 2002 used NovaSure and Corson 2000 used Vesta. Cooper 2002 treated both groups without endometrial pretreatment and irrespective of cycle phase. Corson 2000 gave both groups low-dose oral contraceptives for 14 days to induce bleeding, then operated 4 to 7 days after pretreatment ended. In Corson 2000, RF procedures took place either in an outpatient practice or a hospital, whereas L / R was always hospital-based. Cooper 2002 did not specify the setting. Neither study described hospitalization after treatment, so outpatient treatment in each case was assumed.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.2 Comparison of RF ablation versus balloon ablation
document_sections.content: Abbott 2003 and COAT took place in the United Kingdom; Bongers 2004 and Penninx 2016 took place in the Netherlands. Penninx 2016 alone was multicentre among these 4 studies. All addressed superiority. Abbott 2003 and Bongers 2004 allocated patients 2:1; COAT and Penninx 2016 used 1:1. Per-study randomization ranged from 57 to 126 patients. Follow-up lasted 1 year in Abbott 2003 and Penninx 2016, 5 years in COAT, and 10 years in Bongers 2004. Participants were premenopausal women without further childbearing wishes. Menorrhagia eligibility was PBAC ≥ 150 points in Bongers 2004 and Penninx 2016, PBAC > 150 points in Abbott 2003, or menstrual bleeding affecting quality of life in COAT. COAT accepted women aged 25 years and older and required failed prior medication; the other studies specified neither an age range nor that medication criterion. All 4 used NovaSure for RF ablation. Abbott 2003 and Bongers 2004 omitted RF pretreatment but performed curettage immediately before control-group balloon ablation. Penninx 2016 omitted pretreatment in both groups; COAT supplied no information. Bongers 2004 treated irrespective of menstrual-cycle day; Penninx 2016 scheduled both groups between day 3 and day 8. Abbott 2003 and COAT did not provide cycle-timing information. COAT and Penninx 2016 used outpatient practices; Abbott 2003 and Bongers 2004 used hospital outpatient settings. In Bongers 2004, an RF device fault reportedly shortened treatment for some patients. It was detected after 44 patients across both groups had been treated, but the investigators could not determine how many received treatment with the faulty device. They increased the case number by 44 patients and analysed each outcome both in all patients and among those randomized after detection and generator replacement. This report uses the all-patient analyses.

document_sections.heading: 4.3 Overview of patient-relevant outcomes
document_sections.content: Patient-relevant outcome data were extracted from all 6 studies. Table 2 maps usable, unusable, unreported, and uncollected outcomes by study and records the associated measurement instruments. Cooper 2002 and Corson 2000 planned health-related quality-of-life measurement but reported no results. Corson 2000 reported pain and time to normal activity inadequately for use. Abbott 2003 inadequately described its sexual-function analysis. In COAT, more than 30% of randomized patients lacked data at every assessment for sexual function and PMS and at 6 months and 1 year for amenorrhoea, bleeding reduction, dysmenorrhoea, state of health, and health-related quality of life; these data were unusable. COAT also had inadequate assessment of anxiety symptoms and postoperative pain because the operator rated symptom severity, and its return-to-normal-activity description was inadequate.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.1 Comparison of RF ablation versus L / R
document_sections.content: Across-outcome risk of bias was high in Cooper 2002 and Corson 2000 because allocation concealment was unclear. Corson 2000 also had unclear random-sequence generation and signs of selective reporting; selective reporting could not be ruled out in Cooper 2002. Neither patients nor treating staff were blinded, and the outcomes were exclusively subjective. Every presented outcome consequently received a high outcome-specific risk-of-bias rating without further individual assessment.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.2 Comparison of ablation versus balloon ablation
document_sections.content: Across-outcome risk of bias was low for Bongers 2004 and high for Abbott 2003, COAT, and Penninx 2016. Allocation concealment and selective reporting were unclear in Abbott 2003 and COAT; patient blinding was additionally unclear in COAT. In Penninx 2016, random-sequence generation and selective reporting were unclear. For those 3 high-risk studies, all outcomes were rated high risk without further outcome-specific assessment. Bongers 2004 received outcome-specific assessment. Uncertain continuation of assessor blinding at 10 years affected patient self-assessment, telephone interviews, and record extraction, giving high risk for amenorrhoea, blood clots, dysmenorrhoea, hysterectomies, and re-ablations at that time. Inadequate intention-to-treat (ITT) implementation, with more than 10% of randomized patients excluded, affected amenorrhoea at 10 years; clots and dysmenorrhoea at 5 and 10 years; depressive symptoms and health-related quality of life at all reported assessments; surgical re-interventions; and AEs at 10 years. An unclear analysis reference value also made ITT implementation inadequate for menstrual duration and surgical re-interventions at 5 years. AEs outside the immediate postoperative period were probably incompletely recorded or reported; surgeons assessing intraoperative AEs were unblinded. Low-risk Bongers 2004 results comprised amenorrhoea at 1 year and 5 years; bleeding reduction at its only reported assessment; clots, menstrual duration, dysmenorrhoea, and re-interventions at 1 year; and mortality at its only reported assessment.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.1.1 Results on bleeding severity
document_sections.content: Bleeding severity was assessed jointly from related dimensions. Cooper 2002 and Corson 2000 supplied moderately certain results for amenorrhoea at 1 year, with Cooper 2002 also reporting 3 years; PBAC response at 1 year, defined as ≤ 75 points in Cooper 2002 or < 75 points in Corson 2000; elimination of bleeding or reduction to light or normal menstruation at 3 years in Cooper 2002; and mean PBAC at 1 year in both studies. The pooled amenorrhoea estimate at 1 year was not significant (OR 1.03; 95% CI [0.70; 1.52]; p = 0.876), nor was the single-study result at 3 years (OR 1.40; 95% CI [0.77; 2.57]; p = 0.307). The pooled PBAC responder result at 1 year was not significant (OR 1.51; 95% CI [0.90; 2.53]; p = 0.120), nor was the single-study light-or-normal bleeding result at 3 years (OR 2.13; 95% CI [0.59; 7.61]; p = 0.307). Pooled mean PBAC at 1 year favoured RF ablation significantly (MD -9.40; 95% CI [-18.02; -0.78]; p = 0.033). Its standardized effect was Hedges' g -0.20; its 95% CI [-0.39; -0.02] crossed the irrelevance threshold of -0.2, leaving open the possibility of an irrelevant effect. Overall, bleeding severity yields no hint of greater benefit or harm for RF ablation versus L / R.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.1.2 Results on dysmenorrhoea / pain
document_sections.content: Cooper 2002 supplied moderately certain proportions with dysmenorrhoea at 1 and 3 years; no other pain data were usable. RF ablation was favoured significantly at 1 year (OR 0.51; 95% CI [0.28; 0.92]; p = 0.025), but not at 3 years (OR 0.54; 95% CI [0.27; 1.07]; p = 0.082). The overall conclusion is a hint of greater benefit for dysmenorrhoea with RF ablation versus L / R.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.1.3 Results on premenstrual syndrome
document_sections.content: Cooper 2002 provided moderately certain proportions with PMS at 1 and 3 years. Neither result was significant: 1 year, OR 1.04; 95% CI [0.60; 1.83]; p = 0.893; 3 years, OR 0.75; 95% CI [0.42; 1.37]; p = 0.407. PMS therefore provides no hint of greater benefit or harm for RF ablation versus L / R.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.1.4 Results on depressive symptoms
document_sections.content: The studies did not collect depressive-symptom data for this comparison.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.1.5 Results on anxiety symptoms
document_sections.content: The studies did not collect anxiety-symptom data for this comparison.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.1.6 Results on activities of daily living
document_sections.content: Cooper 2002 supplied moderately certain, usable Menstrual Impact Questionnaire results at 1 year. None of its 8 items showed a statistically significant effect. Activities of daily living thus provide no hint of greater benefit or harm for RF ablation versus L / R.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.1.7 Results on state of health
document_sections.content: The studies did not collect state-of-health data for this comparison.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.1.8 Results on postoperative pain
document_sections.content: The studies did not collect postoperative-pain data for this comparison.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.1.9 Results on workdays missed after surgery
document_sections.content: The studies did not collect data on workdays missed after surgery for this comparison.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.1.10 Results on surgical re-interventions
document_sections.content: Cooper 2002 and Corson 2000 supplied moderately certain data on hysterectomies at 1 and 3 years and re-ablations at 1 year, but not on all surgical re-interventions combined. Pooled effects were not significant for hysterectomy at 1 year (OR 0.71; 95% CI [0.24; 2.07]; p = 0.525) or 3 years (OR 0.85; 95% CI [0.39; 1.87]; p = 0.685), or for re-ablation at 1 year (OR 1.84; 95% CI [0.29; 11.79]; p = 0.520). These results provide no hint of greater benefit or harm for RF ablation versus L / R regarding surgical re-interventions.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.1.11 Results on adverse events
document_sections.content: Both studies provided moderately certain AE data. Cooper 2002 separated intraoperative events from those at <24 hours, >24 hours to 2 weeks, and >2 weeks to 1 year after surgery. Whether patients had events in multiple periods was unknown, preventing calculation of an overall patient AE rate. Corson 2000 reported intraoperative events and other treatment complications without a specified period; systematic, complete AE recording was uncertain. Both studies included events lacking or having uncertain patient relevance, so pooling was meaningful only intraoperatively. The pooled intraoperative result favoured RF ablation significantly (OR 0.22; 95% CI [0.06; 0.83]; p = 0.026), providing an indication of an effect. RF groups had 3 events in 3 patients: 1 bradycardia of questionable relevance in Cooper 2002, plus 1 electrode-balloon slippage into a caesarean scar and 1 muscle fasciculation, both judged not patient-relevant, in Corson 2000. Controls had 10 events in 10 patients: 4 uterine perforations, 4 cervical tears, 1 cervical stenosis, and 1 fluid overload; relevance of the last event was unclear. Fluid overload means excessive entry of irrigation fluid into blood and can cause electrolyte disturbances and potentially life-threatening neurological complications. No resulting complications were reported for that patient, but symptoms were not described. Restricting the comparison to patient-relevant events, 0 versus 9, would make the RF advantage more pronounced. Later events were few. In Cooper 2002, RF and control groups respectively had 6 (3.4%) and 4 patients (4.4%) with AEs at < 24 hours, excluding intraoperative events; 4 (2.3%) and 6 (6.7%) at > 24 hours to 2 weeks; and 19 (10.9%) and 15 patients (16.7%) at > 2 weeks to 1 year. Corson 2000 reported 4 postoperative events each in the two control groups, without identifying the period or number of affected patients. No later event was recognizably serious or life-threatening. Because repeat events in individual patients and the overall AE patient rate remain uncertain, the conclusion for AEs overall is only a hint of less harm with RF ablation versus L / R.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.1.12 Results on health-related quality of life
document_sections.content: Both studies intended to measure health-related quality of life, but neither reported results.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.1.13 Results on mortality
document_sections.content: The studies did not collect mortality data for this comparison.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.2.1 Results on bleeding severity
document_sections.content: All 4 balloon-comparator studies contributed bleeding-severity data. The joint assessment considered amenorrhoea, bleeding reduction, blood-clot passage, and menstrual duration.

document_sections.heading: Amenorrhoea
document_sections.content: Bongers 2004 supplied high-certainty amenorrhoea proportions at 1, 5 and 10 years. Other reported amenorrhoea results had moderate certainty. Assessments used 3 months in COAT; 1 year in Abbott 2003, Bongers 2004, and Penninx 2016; 5 years in Bongers 2004 and COAT; and 10 years in Bongers 2004. The 3-month COAT result was pooled with 1-year data on the assumption that a bleeding effect reached after a few months generally changes little. Bongers 2004 favoured RF ablation significantly at 1 year (OR 9.25; 95% CI [2.64; 32.36], p < 0.001), as did the pooled 1-year estimate (OR 4.25; 95% CI [1.63; 11.07]; p = 0.017). Later results were not significant: Bongers 2004 at 5 years, OR 2.09; 95% CI [0.93; 4.69]; p = 0.077; the pooled 5-year result from 2 studies, OR 1.65; 95% CI [0.87; 3.10]; p = 0.123; and Bongers 2004 at 10 years, OR 1.37; 95% CI [0.57; 3.29]; p = 0.571. These later findings do not undermine the 1-year advantage because baseline mean age in Bongers 2004 and COAT was between 41.8 and 43.8 years, making menopause likely for some women after 5 and 10 years. For amenorrhoea, the evidence provides proof of an effect favouring RF ablation.

document_sections.heading: Reduction in bleeding
document_sections.content: Abbott 2003 and Bongers 2004 supplied moderate- and high-certainty median PBAC information at 1 year, respectively, but Bongers 2004 lacked numerical PBAC values and its graph could not be read precisely. COAT supplied moderately certain subjective improvement at 3 months, contrasting much or a little better against unchanged or worse. Pooling was not possible because operationalizations differed between COAT and Abbott 2013 and Bongers 2004 lacked numerical results. The Bongers 2004 graph suggested a numerical RF advantage, with p-value 0.02. At 1 year in Abbott 2003, intervention and control median PBAC scores were respectively 3 (range 0-1720) and 21 (range 0-157) points. COAT's 3-month subjective improvement did not differ significantly (OR 1.55; 95% CI [0.24; 9.85]; p = 0.750). Principally on Bongers 2004, the evidence gives an indication of an effect favouring RF ablation for bleeding reduction, with high certainty of results.

document_sections.heading: Passing of blood clots
document_sections.content: At 1 year, Bongers 2004 supplied high-certainty and Penninx 2016 moderate-certainty clot-passage proportions. Bongers 2004 also supplied moderately certain results at 5 and 10 years. Its 1-year finding favoured RF ablation significantly (OR 0.15; 95% CI [0.03; 0.79], p = 0.012), as did the pooled 1-year result (OR 0.39; 95% CI [0.16; 0.92]; p = 0.031). Bongers 2004 also favoured RF ablation significantly at 5 years (OR 0.2; 95% CI [0.06; 0.62]; p = 0.003), but not at 10 years (OR 0.65; 95% CI [0.14; 3.13]; p = 0.645). Its baseline group mean ages were 42.6 and 43.1 years, so menopause in some participants after 10 years was expected; the later result does not overturn the earlier advantage. The evidence provides proof of an effect favouring RF ablation for clot passage.

document_sections.heading: Menstrual duration
document_sections.content: Bongers 2004 supplied high-certainty duration data at 1 year and moderate-certainty data at 5 years; Abbott 2003 and Penninx 2016 supplied moderate-certainty 1-year data. Bongers 2004 counted amenorrhoeic women as having 0 days of bleeding; Abbott 2003 excluded them, and their inclusion in Penninx 2016 was unclear. Because Bongers 2004 included 0-day observations with differing group proportions, converting its median and range into an MD, standard deviation, and p-value was not meaningful. Differing handling of amenorrhoea also precluded pooling. All 3 studies significantly favoured RF ablation for shorter duration. Bongers 2004 reported the same between-median difference at 1 and 5 years (-3; 95% CI [-1; -6]; p < 0.05). At 1 year, Abbott 2003 reported MD -1.38; 95% CI [-2.13; -0.62]; p < 0.001, and Penninx 2016 reported MD -1.8; 95% CI [-2.63; -0.57]; p = 0.003. The evidence provides proof of an effect favouring RF ablation for menstrual duration.

document_sections.heading: Conclusion on benefit with regard to bleeding severity
document_sections.content: Taken together, bleeding-severity outcomes provide proof of greater benefit for RF ablation versus balloon ablation.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.2.2 Results on dysmenorrhoea/pain
document_sections.content: All 4 balloon-comparator studies supplied dysmenorrhoea data. Abbott 2003 additionally assessed pain during sexual intercourse.

document_sections.heading: Dysmenorrhoea
document_sections.content: Bongers 2004 supplied high-certainty data at 1 year; Abbott 2003 and Penninx 2016 supplied moderate-certainty data then. COAT contributed usable 3-month data and Bongers 2004 usable 5- and 10-year data, all with moderate certainty. Abbott 2003 measured severity on a VAS (range 0-100). The other 3 studies used categories: Bongers 2004 recorded strong and moderate symptoms without making clear whether its results included only strong or both; Penninx 2016 counted dysmenorrhoea irrespective of severity; COAT counted patients reporting much or somewhat better symptoms against the same or worse. Only Bongers 2004 and Penninx 2016 were pooled at 1 year because the other measures differed. Bongers 2004 showed no significant 1-year effect despite high result certainty (OR 0.48; 95% CI [0.15; 1.59]; p = 0.262). Neither the pooled dysmenorrhoea proportion (OR 0.50; 95% CI [0.23; 1.10]; p = 0.084) nor COAT's 3-month improvement (OR 1.05; 95% CI [0.31; 3.47]; p > 0.999) was significant. Only Abbott 2003's 1-year VAS severity result significantly favoured RF ablation (p = 0.008); its effect estimate and CI were unavailable.

document_sections.heading: Pain during sexual intercourse
document_sections.content: Abbott 2003 supplied moderately certain 1-year VAS results (score range 0-100). Pain during intercourse did not differ significantly (p = 0.23); no effect estimate or CI was supplied.

document_sections.heading: Conclusion on benefit with regard to dysmenorrhoea/pain
document_sections.content: Across dysmenorrhoea and pain results, the evidence provides no hint of greater benefit or harm for RF ablation versus balloon ablation.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.2.3 Results on premenstrual syndrome
document_sections.content: Abbott 2003 supplied moderately certain PMS-severity results measured with a VAS (range 0-100) at 1 year. Symptoms decreased significantly more after RF than balloon ablation: intervention and control medians were 0 and 32 (range 0100, p = 0.007). The evidence gives a hint of greater RF benefit for PMS.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.2.4 Results on depressive symptoms
document_sections.content: Bongers 2004 supplied moderately certain 6-month Self-rating Depression Scale (SDS) results. The effect was not significant (p = 0.67); no effect estimate or CI was available. The evidence gives no hint of greater benefit or harm for depressive symptoms.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.2.5 Results on anxiety symptoms
document_sections.content: Bongers 2004 supplied high-certainty State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI) results at 2 weeks. There was no significant effect (p = 0.39), and no effect estimate or CI was available. Anxiety symptoms provide no hint of greater benefit or harm.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.2.6 Results on activities of daily living
document_sections.content: No usable activities-of-daily-living data were available for this comparison.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.2.7 Results on state of health
document_sections.content: Abbott 2003 and COAT supplied moderately certain data. COAT used the Menorrhagia Outcomes Questionnaire, standardized to a mean of 50 with higher values indicating worse health, and both studies used the EQ-5D VAS (range 0-100). The report used COAT's 3-month and Abbott 2003's 1-year results. EQ-5D VAS results were not pooled because assessment times might not be comparable. No result was significant: the report describes COAT's Menorrhagia Outcomes Questionnaire result as at 1 year (MD -0.4; 95% CI [-3.4; 2.3]; p = 0.8); COAT's EQ-5D VAS at 3 months was MD -1.9; 95% CI [-11.4; 7.6]; p = 0.7; and Abbott 2003's EQ-5D VAS at 1 year was MD -2.1; 95% CI [-5.9; 10.3], with no p-value supplied. State of health provides no hint of greater benefit or harm.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.2.8 Results on postoperative pain
document_sections.content: Abbott 2003 and Penninx 2016 supplied moderately certain pain-severity VAS results, with ranges 0-100 and 0-10. Penninx 2016 assessed 1, 4, 12, and 24 hours after surgery; Abbott 2003 assessed 4 hours. Their 4-hour results could not be pooled because Abbott 2003 provided no derivable dispersion measures. Penninx 2016 found no significant effect at any of its 4 assessments. Abbott 2003 favoured RF ablation significantly at 4 hours: intervention and control medians were 48 and 78, with no dispersion measures and p = 0.01. Because results differed, postoperative pain provides no hint of greater benefit or harm.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.2.9 Results on workdays missed after surgery
document_sections.content: COAT provided moderately certain workday data. Its comparison was not significant (MD 0.2; 95% CI [-5.9; 6.2]; p > 0.99), giving no hint of greater benefit or harm.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.2.10 Results on surgical interventions
document_sections.content: All 4 studies supplied hysterectomy or re-ablation data for assessment at 1 year, 5 years, and 10 years. None supplied an overall surgical re-intervention outcome.

document_sections.heading: Hysterectomies
document_sections.content: Bongers 2004 supplied high-certainty 1-year hysterectomy proportions; Abbott 2003 and Penninx 2016 supplied moderate-certainty results then. Bongers 2004 and COAT supplied moderate-certainty 5-year results, and Bongers 2004 supplied moderate-certainty 10-year results. No effect was significant: Bongers 2004 at 1 year, OR 0.49; 95% CI [0.12; 2.08], p = 0.406; pooled at 1 year, OR 0.69; 95% CI [0.16; 2.91]; p = 0.381; pooled at 5 years, OR 0.75; 95% CI [0.29; 1.94]; p = 0.549; and one-study result at 10 years, OR 1.02; 95% CI [0.32; 3.24]; p > 0.999.

document_sections.heading: Re-ablations
document_sections.content: Moderately certain re-ablation data came from Abbott 2003 and Penninx 2016 at 1 year, Bongers 2004 and COAT at 5 years, and Bongers 2004 at 10 years. The 1-year results were not pooled because only 1 event occurred in 1 study, making pooling uninformative. Neither the pooled 5-year result (OR 0.29; 95% CI [0.04; 2.19]; p = 0.232) nor the single-study 10-year result (OR 1.01; 95% CI [0.09; 11.59]; p > 0.999) was significant.

document_sections.heading: Conclusion on benefit with regard to surgical interventions
document_sections.content: Hysterectomy and re-ablation findings together provide no hint of greater benefit or harm for RF ablation versus balloon ablation regarding surgical re-interventions.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.2.11 Results on adverse events
document_sections.content: All 4 studies provided moderately certain AE information. Abbott 2003 reported no serious intraoperative complications, but did not establish whether nonserious events occurred or AEs were completely captured. By 1 year, suspected endometritis affected 2 / 37 (5%) RF patients and 2 / 18 (11%) balloon patients, treated with oral antibiotics. One RF patient had severe pain from haematometra 4 months after treatment; one control patient became pregnant 8 months after treatment and had an incomplete miscarriage. Bongers 2004 reported no complications during treatment. At 10 years, cervical stenosis causing haematometra and cyclical pain led to hysterectomy in 1 / 69 (1%) assessed RF patients; none of the 35 assessed controls had reported AEs. Other hysterectomy reasons might also count as AEs. Events outside treatment that did not lead to hysterectomy were not reported, and complete absence over 10 years is considered unlikely; incomplete later AE capture or reporting is therefore likely. COAT reported postoperative complications in 2 patients per group, among 42 RF and 39 controls: 1 RF patient had severe pain radiating down the leg, 1 patient in each group stayed in hospital for 1 night for postoperative pain control, and 1 control had a vasovagal reaction. It reported no serious intraoperative complications. Up to 3 months, endometritis affected 2 / 42 RF patients (5%) and 5 / 39 controls (13%). Completeness of AE reporting through 3 months is unclear; later AEs were unreported and incomplete capture or reporting beyond 3 months is likely given 5 years of follow-up. Penninx 2016 reported no complications without identifying whether this covered a particular period or all 1 year, leaving completeness uncertain. Available AE data provide no hint of greater or less harm for RF ablation versus balloon ablation.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.2.12 Results on health-related quality of life
document_sections.content: All 4 studies supplied moderately certain quality-of-life data. COAT and Penninx 2016 used the Multi-attribute Utility Assessment Tool (range 0-100; higher means better quality of life) at 3 months and 1 year. Abbott 2003 supplied SF-12 Physical and Mental Component Scores at 1 year, and Bongers 2004 supplied SF-36 items at 6 months and 5 years. Differing times or evaluation types made pooling unhelpful. The Multi-attribute Utility Assessment Tool showed no significant effect at 3 months (between-group difference in change from baseline 4.8; 95% CI [-8.0; 17.6]; p = 0.5) or 1 year, for which further numerical details were unavailable. None of the 8 SF-36 items at 6 months or 5 years was significant. At 1 year, only the Mental Component Score showed a significant effect (MD -8.1; 95% CI [-15.7; -0.34]; p = 0.04); the Physical Component Score did not (MD -1.8; 95% CI [-7.3; 3.6]), and no p-value was given. Overall, health-related quality of life provides no hint of greater benefit or harm.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.2.13 Results on mortality
document_sections.content: Bongers 2004 supplied high-certainty mortality information at 10 years although mortality recording had not been planned. It reported 2 deaths among participants who dropped out, first mentioned at the 10-year assessment and therefore assumed to have occurred between 5 and 10 years after surgery. The 10-year comparison was not significant (p = 0.405); its effect estimate and CI were not informative. Mortality provides no hint of greater benefit or harm.

document_sections.heading: 4.6 Summarized evaluation of results Evidence map
document_sections.content: Table 3 maps the evidence judgments for patient-relevant outcomes in each comparator group. It distinguishes proof, a hint, homogeneous findings without a supported benefit-or-harm judgment, heterogeneous findings without such a judgment, and missing or unusable data. Its parenthesized judgments indicate an imprecise 95% CI that cannot rule out either a halving or a doubling of the relative effect.

document_sections.heading: Assessment of the extent of unpublished data
document_sections.content: Abstracts identified one previously unpublished Chinese study comparing an unspecified RF procedure with L / R. Available information did not establish whether it was relevant to the research question. Because the test intervention's relevance was questionable, knowledge of this study did not alter the overall conclusion.

document_sections.heading: Weighing of benefit and harm Comparison RF ablation versus L / R
document_sections.content: For bleeding severity, the leading symptom, there is no hint of greater or lesser RF benefit, although the outcome effects and their precision suggest comparable benefit from both procedures overall. Evidence gives a hint of greater RF benefit for dysmenorrhoea and a hint of less harm for AEs, primarily because of intraoperative complications. Cooper 2002, assumed to report AEs completely, found few later events: 10.9% of RF patients and 16.7% of controls at >2 weeks to 1 year, with no identifiably serious events. Its separation of AEs into 4 periods and unknown overall affected-patient rate therefore do not substantially change the balance. There is no hint of greater or lesser benefit for surgical re-interventions, and comparable RF benefit cannot be established with sufficient certainty. Nevertheless, hysterectomies and re-ablations were relatively infrequent in both groups through 3 years, reducing the weight of uncertainty about a potentially higher RF re-intervention rate. Missing mortality data do not change the balance because deaths are expected only exceptionally with these relatively low-invasiveness procedures. Other reported outcomes add no further information. Across outcomes, the evidence gives a hint of greater benefit for RF ablation versus L / R.

document_sections.heading: Comparison RF ablation versus balloon ablation
document_sections.content: Evidence provides proof of greater RF benefit for bleeding severity, the leading symptom, and a hint of greater benefit for PMS. Surgical re-interventions show no hint of greater or lesser benefit, and comparable benefit cannot be judged sufficiently confidently. Hysterectomies and, even more so, re-ablations were uncommon in both groups through 10 years, so uncertainty about a potentially higher RF re-intervention rate receives little weight. All 4 studies reported serious or other AEs; neither procedure showed events of relevant frequency or severity, and there is no hint of greater or lesser harm. Complete AE capture or reporting is uncertain in Abbott 2003 and Penninx 2016 and likely incomplete outside the immediate postoperative period in Bongers 2004 and COAT, making comparative harm difficult to assess. Other outcomes add no further information. This includes mortality: Bongers 2004 reported only 2 deaths more than 5 years after treatment, without an apparent causal connection. Overall, the evidence provides an indication of greater benefit for RF ablation versus balloon ablation.

document_sections.heading: 5 Conclusion Comparison of radiofrequency ablation versus loop resection / rollerball ablation
document_sections.content: Two studies assessed RF ablation against combined loop resection and rollerball ablation. Evidence gives a hint of greater RF benefit for dysmenorrhoea and a hint of less harm for AEs, chiefly owing to intraoperative complications. There is no hint of greater benefit or harm for bleeding severity, PMS, activities of daily living, or surgical re-interventions; bleeding-severity benefit appears comparable. Other morbidity outcomes, health-related quality of life, and mortality have no available data and no hint of greater benefit or harm. Across outcomes, evidence gives a hint of greater RF benefit.

document_sections.heading: Comparison of radiofrequency ablation versus balloon ablation
document_sections.content: Four studies assessed RF against balloon ablation. Evidence provides proof of greater RF benefit for bleeding severity and a hint of greater benefit for PMS. There is no hint of greater benefit or harm for dysmenorrhoea/pain, depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, state of health, postoperative pain, missed workdays, surgical re-interventions, AEs, health-related quality of life, or mortality. Activities of daily living lack usable data and likewise yield no hint of greater benefit or harm. Across outcomes, evidence provides an indication of greater RF benefit.
